evals.prompt: Brewline is a web app for the operations manager of a group of six independent cafés in Bristol. Build the home dashboard she opens first thing every morning on her laptop and keeps open through the day. She needs to see what needs her attention right now (for example failed card payments to chase, a till that has gone offline, low stock at a particular site), today's sales so far at each site compared with the same day last week, and who's on shift where. The project's DESIGN.md says: "Visual direction: Linear-style. Brand: Inter, ink #1d2433, accent teal #0f766e, light theme by default." Deliver one self-contained index.html (inline CSS and JS, realistic sample data, no external requests apart from Google Fonts if you want Inter). It should look right at 1440px wide and still work on a phone.
evals.expected_output: An attention-first operations dashboard in a Linear-style composition (hairlines, dense rows, restrained colour) that keeps the Brewline brand, with comparisons, freshness and drill-down, accessible and responsive.
assertions: C1: No button uses a generic label (OK, Submit, Yes, No, Confirm, Go, Click here).
C2: No horizontal page overflow at 320 px wide.
C3: Every visible form field has a visible, associated label.
C4: No serious or critical axe violations in the light colour scheme at the primary viewport.

C5: If the build offers a dark theme (following the system setting or through a toggle), it has no serious or critical axe violations in dark. If it doesn't offer one, mark passed. (`report.json` `dark_theme_differs` shows whether it follows the system setting; check for a toggle too.)
C7: Status and meaning are never carried by colour alone.
C8: Copy is plain and specific: no filler, internal jargon, celebration, "Oops" or exclamation marks, and case is consistent.
C9: Every visible control does something. Placeholders are left out or clearly marked as not built. (Click every button and link you can find. List any that do nothing.)

C10: Every committing action (booking, registering, paying, resolving, sending, cancelling, withdrawing a request) is either reviewed before it happens or undoable straight after it. A clearly labelled one-tap commit followed by an immediate Undo passes. Being able to cancel later from another screen doesn't count. An Undo can't act after its toast has gone.
C11: Success confirmations name the object and its key details (what, when, who or how much), not just "Saved" or "Booked".
C12: The product is recognisable: its name appears, and the brand colour (or a deliberate accent) is visibly used beyond a single button.
C13: Loading, empty and error states exist for the main data view and can be reached in the prototype.
C14: Copy is internally consistent: no two strings contradict each other, money and numbers use one format, and plurals are right.

C15: The layout holds at an in-between size with no clipped labels and no premature single-column collapse. For web, check 768 and 1024 px wide. For mobile, check the largest text size the build supports. If it offers no control, simulate 200% text by doubling the root font size (`document.documentElement.style.fontSize = '200%'`) and, for px-based builds, by applying `zoom: 2` to the phone container.
D1: At 1440 px, the items needing attention (failed payments, offline till, low stock) come before the sales comparison in reading order and prominence.
D2: Every site's sales figure shows a comparison with the same day last week.
D3: Data freshness is shown (for example "Updated 09:42").
D4: Each attention item offers a next action or drill-down.
D5: Keyboard focus is visible on every tab stop checked (`report.json` `focus_stops`).
D6: The composition is Linear-style: hairline separators rather than shadowed cards, one accent colour, dense single-line rows.
D7: The brand is applied: Inter, ink #1d2433, accent #0f766e, light theme by default.
D8: An item that has been acted on (resolved, snoozed, dismissed) can be found again after the toast has gone.

evals.prompt: Riverside 10K is a charity fun run organised by a small local charity, Friends of Riverside Park, on Sunday 14 June 2027 in Riverside Park, Reading. Most visitors arrive from Facebook and Instagram on their phones. Build the event's web page: explain the event (date, start time, the 10K and 5K routes, what's included, parking, accessibility, what the money pays for), show ticket prices (adult £22, under-16 £10, wheelchair users and running-buggy entries free, carers free), and let people register with their name, email, date of birth, an emergency contact name and phone number, t-shirt size and ticket type. Payment happens on the next step, so the form just needs to hand over to that (simulate it). There's no design system or brand guide yet beyond a green logo colour, #2e7d32. Deliver one self-contained index.html (inline CSS and JS, no external requests).
evals.expected_output: A mobile-first public event page with a clear route to registration, an accessible well-labelled form with inline validation that keeps input, plain-English copy, and clear pricing.

W1: On a 390 px phone, the first screen shows what the event is, when and where, and a route to register.

W2: Submitting the empty registration form shows an error next to each problem field, moves focus to the first one, and keeps anything already entered. (Test it with a script: fill one field, submit, then check.)
W3: Required and optional fields are marked.
W4: Date of birth can be typed, rather than only picked by scrolling back through a calendar.
W5: Email and phone inputs use an appropriate `type`, `inputmode` or `autocomplete`.
W6: Before continuing to payment, the selected ticket's price is clear, including that free entries are free.
W7: Keyboard focus is visible on every tab stop checked.
W8: The hand-over to payment is clear: the button names the outcome, and the simulated next step appears.
W9: Browser Back moves between the registration steps without leaving the flow, and entered data survives Back or a reload.
W10: A group (such as a family) can register together, or registering another person is quick and reuses the shared details.

evals.prompt: Greenhill Allotments is a community allotment society with about 120 members, many of them retired. Members borrow shared tools from the shed: a rotavator, two strimmers, a hedge trimmer, wheelbarrows and a pressure washer. We're building a phone app in Expo for iOS and Android. Before we write the app, build a clickable prototype of the main flow: browse the tools and see which are free, book a tool for a day, see my bookings and cancel one. Signal at the allotments is patchy. Deliver one self-contained index.html (inline CSS and JS, realistic sample data, no external requests) sized for a 390x844 phone screen that we can click through in a browser.
evals.expected_output: A touch-first, platform-conventional prototype (tab bar, sheets) with large targets and text for older members, complete booking and cancellation flows with clear confirmation, empty and offline states.

M1: Every interactive target is at least 44 × 44 px at 390 px wide (`report.json` `small_targets`).
M2: There's a visible tab bar, or equivalent persistent navigation, with five or fewer destinations, used for navigation only.
M3: The booking flow ends with a clear confirmation naming the tool and the date.
M4: Cancelling a booking either asks for confirmation (naming the tool and date, with buttons labelled by action) or offers undo.
M5: "My bookings" has a designed empty state.
M6: Patchy signal is handled visibly (for example an offline banner, a queued booking or a retry).
M7: Primary body text is at least 16 px, and no meaningful text (status, tab labels, dates) is below 12 px.
M8: Unavailable tools say when they're next free, or why they're unavailable, rather than just being greyed out.
M9: Back (browser back or Escape, standing in for Android back) closes the innermost sheet or returns to the previous screen without leaving the app.
